<article>
Indonesia: Dozens dead after earthquake off Flores island
Shakeel Sobhan, Karl Sexton, with AFP, AP, Reuters | DW, August 15, 2026

At least 47 people have died and several buildings were damaged after the powerful magnitude 7.7 earthquake, which was followed by dozens of aftershocks. A tsunami warning has been lifted.

A powerful earthquake struck off the coast of Indonesia early on Saturday, killing at least 47 people and toppling buildings, the National Disaster Mitigation Agency said.

The epicenter of the magnitude 7.7 earthquake hit off the coast of the island of Flores at a shallow depth of 10 kilometers (6.2 miles), the US Geological Survey (USGS) said.

Shallow earthquakes (up to 70 kilometers deep) are considered more dangerous and destructive.

Tsunami waves of less than 1 meter (3 feet) were recorded in several areas of the country before the warning was lifted about three hours after the quake.

Where did the earthquake strike?

Indonesia's Meteorology, Climatology, and Geophysics Agency (BMKG) recorded the first quake at 4:58 am (2158 GMT) at a depth of 15 km (9 miles), followed by dozens of aftershocks.

People rushed out onto the street as the quake struck.

Video shared on social media from Maumere, the main town in Sikka Regency on Flores Island in eastern Indonesia, showed part of a building collapsing in a cloud of dust and rubble as people screamed and ran into the street.

"Many buildings here were damaged ... I saw that the waiting room at the Pelni port terminal in Maumere had collapsed," Yohanna Embu, a resident of Sikka, a regency within East Nusa Tenggara province, told AP.

Residents evacuated, tsunami warning lifted

The initial jolt was followed by a series of aftershocks in the same area, including one of magnitude 6.1.

BMKG issued a tsunami warning for part of East Nusa Tenggara, West Nusa Tenggara, South Sulawesi and Southeast Sulawesi provinces, urging residents to stay away from beaches and riverbanks.

The tsunami warning was later lifted.

"We have ended (the tsunami warning) but we will keep monitoring the sea level," Wijayanto, earthquake and tsunami director at BMKG, said.

Before the tsunami warning was lifted, residents of Maumere on Flores Island were told to move to higher ground, according to AFP.

State television also showed hundreds of people evacuating in nearby Nagekeo regency.

Local TV footage showed a hospital in the district of Ende in East Nusa Tenggara Province moving patients outside.

Authorities assessing damage, casualties

The quake caused severe damage and collapsed buildings, causing power outages in cities and villages, severely hindering rescue operations.

"We are continuing to collect reports of damages and casualties, but there are communication disruptions," East Nusa Tenggara police chief Rudi Darmoko said.

Local television reports showed patients at several hospitals being evacuated from buildings as a precaution.

"Our students and nuns ran out in panic beneath a collapsing roof," Guidelbertus Tanga, rector of Ritapiret Seminary on Flores said. "At least one priest suffered a broken leg after jumping from the second floor of a building during the quake."

There were also damages reported in some part of southern Sulawesi island.

Why does Indonesia keep getting hit by major earthquakes?

Indonesia is located on the so-called "Ring of Fire," a region of heightened seismic activity in the Pacific basin that stretches from Southeast Asia to Japan.

Here are some of the biggest earthquakes to strike the region:

1992, magnitude 7: A tsunami following a strong earthquake on the southeastern island of Flores killed about 2,500 people.

2004, magnitude 9.1: A quake struck off the coast of Sumatra triggering a tsunami that killed 170,000 in Indonesia and 220,000 in several countries in the Indian Ocean.

2018, magnitude 6.9: A tremor killed more than 550 people on the islands of Lombok and Sumbawa.

2018, magnitude 7.5: A quake and a subsequent tsunami in Palu on Sulawesi island left more than 4,300 people dead or missing.
</article>

Hawk Fire spreads near Reno, 42,000 ordered to evacuate

RENO, Nevada (AP) — A fast-growing wildfire that began Saturday in the hills northwest of Reno had burned more than 15,000 acres by late Sunday with zero containment, and Nevada Governor Joe Lombardo declared a state of emergency in Washoe County.

The Hawk Fire was first reported around 11:25 a.m. Saturday near Hawk Meadow Trail in the Peavine Peak area of the Humboldt-Toiyabe National Forest, where rugged foothills ringed by homes and businesses sit near the California state line. Officials attributed the fire to human causes.

"Please heed all warnings from local officials, evacuate immediately if you are ordered to do so, and do not put yourself or first responders at risk."

The declaration directs all state agencies to work through the Nevada Emergency Operations Center, and the governor authorized one CH-47 Chinook helicopter, one UH-60 Black Hawk and 72 National Guard security personnel to support the response.

US Highway 395 was closed between Parr Boulevard and Red Rock Road as the fire line shifted.

US national debt tops $40 trillion for the first time

WASHINGTON (Reuters) — Total US debt has topped $40 trillion for the first time, the Treasury Department said on Wednesday, drawing fresh warnings that a fiscal crisis is brewing as ballooning costs for social safety-net programs and interest payments far outstrip revenues held back by tax cuts.

The Treasury's latest daily cash and debt balances statement showed total public debt outstanding at $40.047 trillion on Tuesday, a total that includes Treasury securities held by the public of $32.266 trillion and intra-governmental debt holdings of $7.782 trillion.

The milestone has arrived faster than forecasters expected. A decade ago, the national debt stood at about $19.4 trillion, so the government's total borrowing has more than doubled in ten years.

The Congressional Joint Economic Committee calculated that the debt is now growing at roughly $90,000 every second. At a population of about 343 million, the $40 trillion total works out to approximately $117,000 per person.

Treasury also reported a $432.3 billion deficit for July, the highest monthly total in more than five years, with the year-to-date shortfall nearing $1.8 trillion.

The Washington Post reported that the landmark figure was reached months earlier than some models predicted, in part because of billions of dollars in lost revenue from President Donald Trump's invalidated tariffs.

The public share of the debt is now near 100 percent of GDP, and the total passed $30 trillion just four and a half years ago.
</article>

US launches 'Operation Economic Outcast' against Iran

WASHINGTON (AP) — Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday announced a new campaign of financial sanctions against Iran, warning every country that does business with the Islamic Republic to sever those ties or face retaliation from the United States.

Bessent dubbed the campaign "Operation Economic Outcast" and an "economic D-Day," likening it to the Allied landings in France in the Second World War. "Our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone," he said.

China, Turkey and the United Arab Emirates are Iran's largest trade partners. Ahead of Monday's announcement, the United Arab Emirates said it was ending all trade relations with Iran.

Lake Kariba ferry disaster: death toll rises to 80

HARARE (AP) — The death toll from an overloaded ferry that capsized on Lake Kariba in Zimbabwe last week rose to 80 after eight more bodies were recovered on Sunday, police said.

The government-run passenger ferry, the Mbuya Nehanda, overturned in choppy water on Tuesday while travelling from the town of Kariba toward rural and fishing communities in the country's northwest, where roads are damaged and public transport is scarce. The town of Kariba sits nearly 280 kilometres northwest of the capital, Harare, and the ferry was a vital link for the rural communities living around the lake, which shares its waters with Zambia.

<article>
Bangladesh elects its president in first contested vote in 35 years

DHAKA (AP) — Bangladesh's parliament on Thursday elected ruling party veteran Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir as the country's 23rd president in the first contested presidential election in 35 years.

Alamgir, 78, a stalwart of the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), won with 255 votes, defeating Colonel (retd) Oli Ahmed, 84, the chairman of the Liberal Democratic Party and the nominee of the 11-party opposition alliance led by Jamaat-e-Islami, who received 88 votes. Of the 349 members of parliament eligible to vote, 343 cast ballots, and the chief election commissioner, AMM Nasir Uddin, declared Alamgir the winner.

Every presidential election since the country became a parliamentary democracy in October 1991 had been uncontested.

The post fell vacant last month following the resignation of the former president, Mohammed Shahabuddin, who stepped down for health reasons. The former president was a close ally of ousted Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina.

Alamgir has served as the BNP's secretary-general since 2016 and as minister of local government before the party returned to power in the February 2026 election. After receiving the party's nomination last week, he stepped down as secretary-general and resigned from the party's National Standing Committee.

The president's role in Bangladesh is largely constitutional and ceremonial, while executive authority rests with the government headed by Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, who was sworn in on February 17.

Alamgir took the oath of office on Friday at the Darbar Hall of Bangabhaban, the presidential palace. His election has reopened debate over the party whip system under Article 70 of the constitution.
</article>

<article>
Central African Republic closes gold mine that killed more than 100

BANGUI (AP) — The Central African Republic's government on Saturday shut down a gold mining site that killed more than 100 people when it collapsed earlier this week, citing non-compliance with regulatory procedures.

Ruffin Benam Beltoungou, the minister of mines and geology, announced the closure of the Zamboye site in the western part of the country, citing "non-compliance with mining standards and non-compliance with administrative directives," as an investigation continues.

The artisanal mine caved in Tuesday in the village of Zamboye, near the border with Cameroon. Local officials and the Red Cross said Wednesday that more than 100 people had died in the collapse and warned the toll was likely to rise, while the mines ministry put the official toll at 49, a breakdown of 34 Central Africans, 13 Cameroonians and two Chadians.

The minister visited the site on Wednesday. Seven injured people were taken to a hospital in Baboua, about 50 kilometres from the mining site, and rescue operations were at times suspended because the mine continued to collapse and heavy rains had flooded lower sections of the pit.

The site, locally known as Moscow-RCA, is a sprawling open-pit mine beside the Kadei River, which forms part of the border with Cameroon, and thousands of people in the area depend on it. The Zamboye site had been closed before the accident, but illegal miners still worked there.

The Baboua prosecutor's office opened a judicial investigation to establish the cause of the collapse and who was running the site. Search for survivors by local workers was hampered by a lack of expertise and equipment for the scale of the disaster.

Merck, Moderna say personalized mRNA vaccine met goals in late-stage melanoma trial

RAHWAY, N.J. (Reuters) — Moderna and Merck said on Wednesday that a personalized mRNA cancer vaccine reduced the risk of melanoma returning or spreading in a late-stage trial, a milestone in a new field of cancer treatment that sent Moderna's shares surging as much as 160%.

The companies announced positive topline results from the Phase 3 INTerpath-001 trial evaluating intismeran autogene, an mRNA-based individualized neoantigen therapy, in combination with Merck's immunotherapy Keytruda (pembrolizumab), compared with Keytruda alone.

At a pre-specified interim analysis, the combination demonstrated statistically significant and clinically meaningful improvements in the primary endpoint of recurrence-free survival (RFS) and the key secondary endpoint of distant metastasis-free survival (DMFS) in patients with completely resected stage IIB-IV cutaneous melanoma who had not received prior systemic therapy.

The trial enrolled 1,137 patients, randomized 2:1 to receive intismeran, dosed every three weeks for up to nine doses, with Keytruda every six weeks for up to nine cycles, versus Keytruda alone for approximately one year. The study will continue to evaluate other key endpoints, including overall survival.

This is the first positive Phase 3 readout for an individualized neoantigen therapy and for an mRNA-based cancer therapy, the companies said. The data will be presented at an upcoming international medical meeting, and the partners plan to engage with regulators on filing submissions.

Moderna President Stephen Hoge said thousands of patients who have undergone surgery to remove high-risk melanoma tumors could benefit as soon as next year if regulators approve the vaccine.

The Phase 3 results build on five-year follow-up data from the Phase 2b KEYNOTE-942 trial, presented at the 2026 ASCO Annual Meeting, in which the combination reduced the risk of recurrence or death by 49% and the risk of distant metastasis or death by 59% compared with Keytruda alone.

Merck and Moderna have been research partners since 2016. Merck paid $200 million upfront to begin the alliance and $250 million in 2022 to exercise its option for intismeran.
</article>

<article>
Ebola outbreak in DR Congo becomes deadliest in its history

KINSHASA (AFP) — The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo has killed 2,325 people, surpassing the death toll of the 2018-2020 outbreak to become the deadliest in the country's history, public health officials said on Sunday.

DR Congo's Institute of Public Health said it had recorded 4,945 confirmed cases, including 101 in the previous 24 hours. The latest government data shows that the total number of deaths has surpassed the 2,299 deaths recorded in the 2018-2020 outbreak, which was previously the country's worst on record.

The outbreak, declared by national authorities on 15 May, is the 17th to have emerged in DR Congo since Ebola was discovered 50 years ago. It became the country's largest in terms of total confirmed cases in late July, and researchers say it may have been spreading undetected since February.

It is the fastest-growing outbreak in the known history of the virus: the world's deadliest, in West Africa in 2014-2016, took close to five months to reach 1,000 fatalities, while the current outbreak reached 2,000 deaths in under three months. The World Health Organization has said the outbreak is on track to surpass the 2014-2016 outbreak, which killed 11,325 people across Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone.

The outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo strain. As of 19 August, the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control reported 5,290 confirmed cases and 2,516 deaths, with 837 people hospitalised in Ituri, North Kivu and Haut-Uele provinces. The virus has spread to Uganda, and Europe has recorded its first imported case.

Infections among health workers continue, with at least 155 confirmed cases, including 45 deaths.

On Thursday, the UN's International Coordinating Group, led by the WHO, allocated 70,000 doses of the Ervebo vaccine, developed by Merck, to DR Congo. Ervebo is approved for the Zaire strain, used in the 2018 and 2020 DRC outbreaks, and has not been evaluated against Bundibugyo, the strain in this outbreak, so the doses will be used in a Phase 3 trial of the Zaire vaccine against Bundibugyo. The ICG had already allocated 56,000 Ervebo doses for DRC outbreaks between 2021 and July 2026.
</article>

Zelenskyy wrote that a Russian missile attack on Kryvyi Rih killed two people and wounded 14 others, and that one more person had been killed in the city of Sumy.
